slides.title: Pap test (cervical cytology)
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Cervical cells collected with a brush or spatula (smear or liquid-based vial)

What it is used for: The Pap test screens for cervical cancer: it aims to find precancerous changes before symptoms appear, so treatment can prevent cancer. It also helps find cancer early, when it is easier to treat, and sometimes shows infection or inflammation.

US recommendations (as summarised by NCI): USPSTF — Pap test every 3 years at ages 21–29; at 30–65, an HPV test every 5 years, an HPV/Pap cotest every 5 years, or a Pap test every 3 years. ACS — an HPV test every 5 years from 25 to 65 (cotest every 5 years or Pap every 3 years remain acceptable). After 65, with regular normal results, screening is usually no longer needed. HIV, a weakened immune system or a recent abnormal result may call for more frequent screening.

slides.title: Pap test (cervical cytology)
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Cervical cancer develops slowly: first, abnormal changes called dysplasia appear in the cells; if not removed, they may become cancer over time. Long-lasting infection with high-risk HPV types causes almost all cervical cancers.
Besides the conventional smear there is liquid-based cytology (for example ThinPrep); one advantage is that HPV testing can be done on the same preparation, one disadvantage is higher cost.

slides.title: Pap test (cervical cytology)
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Interpreting the result · 1/2
bullets: Cytology and histology terms correspond: LSIL on a Pap test is generally CIN 1 on biopsy, and HSIL can be CIN 2, CIN 2/3 or CIN 3. CIN 1 often goes away on its own; CIN 3 is not cancer but may become cancer if untreated.

slides.title: Pap test (cervical cytology)
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Interpreting the result · 2/2
bullets: An abnormal result does not mean cancer. For ASC-US an HPV test is usually done. Next steps follow ASCCP risk-based guidelines, weighing current and past results, prior treatment and age: a repeat test in 1 or 3 years, colposcopy with biopsy, or treatment.

slides.title: Pap test (cervical cytology)
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: For 2 days before the test, avoid vaginal sex, douching, vaginal medicines and spermicidal foam or cream; MedlinePlus also advises avoiding tampons. Sources differ on periods: MedlinePlus advises not testing during your period (about 5 days after it ends is a good time), while CDC says both tests can still be done during a period — follow your provider's or laboratory's instructions.

Limitations: A single Pap test detects high-grade lesions with a sensitivity of 55–80%; a programme of regular testing is likely more sensitive. False positives can lead to unnecessary follow-up and procedures, and false negatives can delay care.

A Pap test does not diagnose cancer — colposcopy and biopsy do. Pap tests have no use for diagnosing bacterial vaginosis; trichomonads may be seen incidentally on a Pap smear, but that is not diagnostic and should be confirmed with a sensitive test.

slides.title: Human papillomavirus (HPV) test
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Cervical cells (clinician-collected) or a self-collected vaginal swab

What it is used for: The HPV test looks in a sample of cervical cells for the infection that causes precancer and cancer. It is done alone (primary screening), with a Pap test (cotesting), or after an abnormal Pap — for example, ASC-US, to see whether HPV caused the changes. The screening schedule is on the Pap test card.

Physiology: HPV is a group of more than 200 related viruses: low-risk types cause warts, while high-risk types can cause cervical, anal, oropharyngeal, vulvar, vaginal and penile cancers. The test detects DNA or RNA from high-risk HPV. HPV usually spreads through sexual contact, is especially common at ages 21–29, and usually clears on its own within a year or two.

slides.title: Human papillomavirus (HPV) test
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Interpreting the result
bullets: Positive result: A positive result means high-risk HPV was found. It does not mean you have or will get precancer or cancer, but it raises future risk. There is no treatment for the HPV infection itself; next steps (colposcopy, more frequent testing) depend on past results, age and other factors.

Positive result: A positive test after several negative ones is not necessarily a new infection: HPV can become active again after many years. Whether a reactivated infection carries the same risk as a new one is not known.
Negative result: A negative result means high-risk HPV was not found. Per NCI, the next test is in 5 years; you may need to return sooner if you had abnormal results in the past.

slides.title: Human papillomavirus (HPV) test
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: The sample is taken by the provider from the cervix with a speculum and soft brush, or self-collected in a clinic by inserting and rotating a swab in the vagina. An HPV test alone needs no preparation. For 2 days before a cotest, avoid vaginal sex, douching, vaginal medicines and spermicides; tell the provider about recent sex or a period.

A Pap smear (cotest) is not done during a period — about 5 days after it ends is a good time; for 2 days before, avoid tampons, vaginal creams and medicines, douching and vaginal sex. An HPV test alone needs no preparation; tell the provider if you have your period. The textbook advises stopping vaginal suppositories 2–3 days before.
Limitations: HPV vaccination does not prevent infection with all high-risk types, so vaccinated people should still be screened.

slides.title: Human papillomavirus (HPV) test
slides.eyebrow: Cytology and smears · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Self-collected HPV testing may improve access to screening; in a pooled analysis of studies in China, however, self-collected samples were less sensitive for CIN 2+ (about 86%) than physician-collected samples (about 97%).

slides.title: Superficial squamous cell
slides.caption:
1 — Broad, flat, polygonal cytoplasm.
2 — Small, dense (pyknotic) nucleus.
What it looks like: Large, thin, polygonal cell. Pink-orange (eosinophilic) cytoplasm. Very small, dark, dense — pyknotic — nucleus.
Key feature: Tiny dot-like dark nucleus + pink cytoplasm.
What it means: The most mature epithelial layer. Present in a normal smear; predominance reflects oestrogen effect.
Confused with: Intermediate cell — larger vesicular nucleus, bluish cytoplasm.
Stain / preparation: Papanicolaou (Pap)
Caveat: Often pink, but staining colour varies.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Intermediate squamous cell
slides.caption:
1 — Broad, usually blue-green cytoplasm.
2 — Vesicular nucleus, larger than in a superficial cell.
What it looks like: Large polygonal cell, edges often folded. Blue-green (cyanophilic) cytoplasm. Medium vesicular nucleus with fine chromatin.
Key feature: Its nucleus is the "ruler" other nuclei are compared with.
What it means: The main cell of a normal smear.
Stain / preparation: Papanicolaou (Pap)
Caveat: A handy nuclear reference; size varies with preparation and condition.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Parabasal cell
slides.caption:
1 — Smaller round or oval cells with dense cytoplasm.
2 — Larger nuclear share than intermediate and superficial cells.
What it looks like: Smaller, round or oval. Dense blue-green cytoplasm. Relatively large nucleus.
Key feature: Round shape and dense cytoplasm.
What it means: Deep epithelial layer. Many of them suggest low oestrogen (menopause, postpartum) — an atrophic smear.
Confused with: Metaplastic cell, HSIL cell — look at the nucleus.
Stain / preparation: Papanicolaou (Pap)
Caveat: A parabasal cell with a regular nucleus is not HSIL.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Endocervical (columnar) cells
slides.caption:
1 — En face: an orderly honeycomb sheet.
2 — Side view: columnar cells with basal nuclei.
What it looks like: En face — a "honeycomb" sheet. Side view — tall cells with basal nuclei in a row ("picket fence").
Key feature: Honeycomb or picket fence.
What it means: From the endocervical canal. Their presence shows the transformation zone was sampled (specimen adequacy).
Stain / preparation: Papanicolaou (Pap)
Caveat: Two views of the same epithelium; not all cells are ciliated.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Squamous metaplastic cell
slides.caption:
1 — Dense cytoplasm; round or oval, usually regular nucleus.
2 — Some cells show an angular outline or cytoplasmic process.
What it looks like: Medium size, dense blue-green cytoplasm, often with processes ("spider" cell). Oval, smooth nucleus.
Key feature: Cytoplasmic processes.
What it means: From the transformation zone; a normal finding.
Stain / preparation: Papanicolaou (Pap)
Caveat: Not identified by processes alone; appearance changes with maturation.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Koilocyte
slides.caption:
Refer to a physician / haematologist
1 — A sharply bordered, irregular perinuclear cavity (halo).
2 — Enlarged dark nucleus with an irregular outline; dense cytoplasm at the rim.
What it looks like: A large clear perinuclear cavity with a sharp edge (halo) and a dense cytoplasmic rim. Enlarged, dark, irregular ("raisinoid") nucleus, often binucleate.
Key feature: Halo + abnormal nucleus. A plain nucleus means it is not one.
What it means: A sign of HPV effect; reported as LSIL in Bethesda.
Confused with: Small perinuclear clearing (glycogen, inflammation) — vague edge and a normal nucleus.
Stain / preparation: Papanicolaou (Pap)
Caveat: A halo alone is not enough: nuclear atypia must be present.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: HSIL: high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion
slides.caption:
Refer to a physician / haematologist
1 — High nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, scant cytoplasm.
2 — Irregular nuclear outline, coarse dark chromatin.
What it looks like: Small immature cells, often in groups. The nucleus fills most of the cell; dark, irregular, coarse chromatin.
Key feature: High nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio. Compare with an intermediate nucleus.
What it means: High likelihood of a precancerous lesion. The clinician decides next steps per ASCCP 2019 — colposcopy or expedited treatment. The cytologist reports.
Confused with: Parabasal and metaplastic cells — smooth nuclei, fine chromatin.
Stain / preparation: Papanicolaou (Pap)
Caveat: The drawing explains HSIL features; a cytologist makes the final call.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: The Bethesda System (2014)
rows: Negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy
Normal. Organisms and reactive changes are reported separately.
Atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance
The commonest equivocal result; usually triaged with an HPV test.
Usually HPV effect (koilocytes); often regresses. The clinician decides next steps.
Atypical squamous cells, cannot exclude HSIL
A high-grade lesion is possible — colposcopy is usual.
High likelihood of precancer. The clinician decides next steps per ASCCP 2019 — colposcopy or expedited treatment (without prior biopsy).

slides.title: The Bethesda System (2014)
rows: Atypical glandular cells (endocervical, endometrial or not otherwise specified — NOS)

Glandular abnormality; the clinician decides the work-up (ASCCP 2019, non-pregnant patients: colposcopy with endocervical sampling; at age 35 or older, and under 35 at increased risk of endometrial neoplasia — e.g. abnormal uterine bleeding, signs of chronic anovulation or obesity — endometrial sampling as well; for atypical endometrial cells, endometrial and endocervical sampling first).
Atypical glandular cells, favor neoplastic (endocervical or not otherwise specified)
Falls short of AIS or adenocarcinoma, but neoplasia is likely. The clinician decides the work-up per ASCCP 2019.
Adenocarcinoma (endocervical, endometrial, extrauterine or not otherwise specified — NOS)
Malignant glandular cells — urgent specialist referral.

slides.title: Reference values and decision limits
rows: menstruating woman (depends on cycle phase), smear from the proximal part of the lateral vaginal wall
menstruating woman, smear from the proximal part of the lateral vaginal wall
from age 30 a high-performance (HPV) test every 5–10 years; in people living with HIV from age 25 every 3–5 years years
slides.footnote: The reference interval varies by laboratory, method and population; the laboratory verifies its own interval (verification).

slides.title: Pap result: ASC-US. Per NCI, what is the usual next step?
options: Do nothing and repeat in 10 years
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: ASC-US is the most common abnormal finding; an HPV test shows whether HPV is the cause.

slides.title: A Pap smear has too few cells, hidden by mucus. What is this result called?
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: NCI: unsatisfactory — too few cells, or cells hidden by blood or mucus; repeat in 2–4 months.

Fundamentals of cytological examination. Importance of cytological examination in the diagnosis of neoplastic diseases?
bullets: 1. Cytology is making a diagnosis from the structure of cells: exfoliative (naturally shed or washing/brushing) and aspiration (fine needle aspirate) material.
2. Advantages: minimally invasive, rapid, inexpensive, repeatable; screening (cervix), early detection of tumors, assessing spread (fluids, lymph nodes), monitoring treatment effect.

3. Criteria of malignancy: nuclear enlargement and pleomorphism, increased N/C ratio, hyperchromasia and uneven chromatin, irregular nuclear membrane, prominent/multiple nucleoli, atypical mitoses, cell overlap and mutual "molding", loss of cohesion.
4. Limitations: does not show tissue architecture (invasion is hard to determine), specimen adequacy and reactive changes are sources of error; if needed, confirm with histology.

slides.title: Fundamentals of cytological examination. Importance of cytological examination in the diagnosis of neoplastic diseases?
bullets: 5. Additional methods: cell block, immunocytochemistry (for example TTF-1, p40, calretinin), molecular tests (HPV, mutations), liquid-based cytology.

slides.title: General information about tumors. Cytodiagnosis of malignant tumors?
bullets: 1. A tumor is a collection of clonal cells with uncontrolled proliferation; benign (mature, expansive growth, no metastasis) and malignant (immature, infiltrative growth, metastasis) tumors; epithelial (carcinomas), mesenchymal (sarcomas), hematopoietic (leukemias, lymphomas), etc.

2. Cytological signs of malignant tumors: cell and nuclear pleomorphism, increased N/C ratio, hyperchromasia, uneven chromatin, large/multiple nucleoli, atypical mitoses, loss of cohesion, necrotic background ("diathesis").

3. Signs of histogenetic type: squamous cell carcinoma (keratinization, "fiber" and "tadpole" cells), adenocarcinoma (glandular structures, vacuolated cytoplasm, eccentric nucleus), small cell carcinoma (small "molded" nuclei, scant cytoplasm), lymphoma (diffusely scattered monotonous lymphoid cells).

slides.title: General information about tumors. Cytodiagnosis of malignant tumors?
bullets: 4. Differentiation from reactive atypia (inflammation, regeneration, radiation) is a source of error; in doubtful cases the category "suspicious for malignancy" and histological confirmation.
5. Immunocytochemistry and molecular tests help to determine the origin of the tumor.

slides.title: Cytodiagnosis of tumors of the respiratory organs?
bullets: 1. Material: sputum (morning, several days), bronchial wash and brushing, bronchoalveolar lavage, transbronchial and EBUS-TBNA aspirates, pleural fluid.
2. Squamous cell carcinoma: keratinized, with dense orange cytoplasm (Pap), pleomorphic cells, hyperchromatic pyknotic nuclei; immunophenotype p40+.

3. Adenocarcinoma: groups and glandular/papillary structures, vacuolated cytoplasm, eccentric nuclei, prominent nucleoli; TTF-1 and Napsin-A positive; preserve material for molecular tests (EGFR, ALK, etc.).
4. Small cell carcinoma: small cells with scant cytoplasm, nuclei "molded" to each other, fine chromatin, crush artifact; neuroendocrine markers.
5. Sensitivity depends on the material and tumor location: for central tumors sputum and washings are more effective, for peripheral ones – guided aspiration; EBUS-TBNA in diagnosis and staging.

slides.title: Cytodiagnosis of tumors of the respiratory organs?
bullets: 6. Differentiation from reactive changes (metaplasia, regeneration, viruses).
